newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Manila shares drop on Ramos surgery, Asia mixed.
newsitem.headline: Manila shares drop on Ramos surgery, Asia mixed.

text.p: The Philippine stock market dropped more than one percent on Monday on news that President Fidel Ramos underwent surgery while Hong Kong's bourse leapt by 1.5 percent buoyed by Wall Street.
Other Asian markets were generally mixed, with trade in many Asian financial centres quiet due to the holiday season.
The Tokyo stock market was closed for a national holiday. It will reopen on Tuesday.
Philippine financial markets, expecting a slow Christmas week, were shaken by news that Ramos, 68, underwent surgery to clear a blocked artery, brokers and traders said.
Although the 75-minute operation was successfully concluded by the time markets opened, there was a big stock sell-off, they said.
The stock market plunged more than two percent at the opening but recovering marginally after doctors announced that the operation was successful.
The bourse's composite index slid 40.28 points or 1.27 percent closing at 3,139.92 points in moderate trade. It had plunged to 3,112.56 points earlier in the day.
Hong Kong stocks bounded ahead to close higher, with buying fueled by the recent turnaround on Wall Street and an improved outlook for the local real estate market, brokers said.
"Wall Street turned around, so Hong Kong has a squeeze on the short positions," said Andrew To, dealing director at OSK Asia Securities.
The Hang Seng Index closed 200.07 points or 1.52 percent higher at 13,331.48 after touching a high of 13,361.24.
"The Dow Jones Industrial Average turned around so dramatically. Now it is trading about 100 points below the historical high. So the whole situation changed," added To.
The Dow ended 10.76 points up at 6,484.40 in volatile trade on Friday, gaining nearly 200 points in a week.

Singapore shares slipped back slightly at the close, unmoved by news late in the trading day that the country would hold general elections on January 2. The Straits Times Industrials Index closed 2,195.86, down just 0.95 points.
Taiwan share prices closed higher on news that the finance ministry would sell off its holdings in the "big three" state commercial banks by July 1997 to ease a state budget deficit.
The ministry holds only small stakes in Chang Hwa, First Bank and Hua Nan, which are controlled by Taiwan's provincial government and will remain in state hands after the selloff.
The weighted index ended 31.51 points or 0.46 percent higher at 6,932.00, but somewhat back from a 6,954.73 morning high.

Malaysian shares closed broadly lower on thin volume and a lack of investor interest, dealers and analysts said. The Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks ended 5.28 points or 0.44 percent lower at 1,197.78.
Jakarta shares ended slightly up on a rise in heavyweight Telkom. The Jakarta Composite Index rose 0.55 points or 0.09 percent to close at 633.07.

Australian shares edged to a slightly higher close with light buying interest in the bank sector supporting the market as it wound down for the festive season. The All Ordinaries index closed 6.7 points or 0.28 percent higher at 2,380.5.
Lead stock Telecom lead a lethargic New Zealand share market lower. The top 40 index fell 6.17 or 0.26 percent to 2343.81.
Seoul's composite stock index ended down 8.33 points or 1.20 percent to provisionally close at 684.81.
Thai stocks reversed steep losses late in the day, the SET Index closing up 3.00 points or 0.37 percent at 819.79.
Hong Kong gold bullion ended at US$368.40/90 an ounce against New York's US$368.30/80 close on Friday.
At 1037 GMT, the dollar traded at 114.11/21 yen and 1.5537/44 marks.

Brent crude futures fell slightly during Asian hours, undermined by a continued slide of NYMEX futures. February Brent on SIMEX was last traded at $23.39 per barrel, down seven cents from London, on just 34 lots.
